blocks.text: The first generation of New Zealand web GIS had already reduced the need for installed specialist software. PHEW!, Census WebMap, council viewers, DOCgis and other early web systems let people reach maps through browsers. That was a substantial change, but many of those applications still behaved like GIS viewers. They were designed around the map and the layers available through it. The user generally began by deciding what to display, where to navigate and what to inspect.

blocks.text: The Crown Forestry Rental Trust had already been using digital mapping in Treaty work before the Whanganui ArcFlax DVD appeared. In November 2004 the Trust publicly confirmed that it was using three-dimensional mapping technology to assist Māori claimants and the Waitangi Tribunal. The Tribunal’s bibliography separately identifies several Trust-commissioned thematic and land-block map books from 2005, covering Central North Island inquiries, Te Urewera and other districts. Those were documented mapping products prepared to support hearings, while the 2006 ArcFlax edition was catalogued as an interactive DVD for viewing GIS information. The surviving records describe three related kinds of work, but do not establish a single software platform or identical underlying map layers across them.

blocks.text: An archived presentation titled “ESRI 2005 – Participatory GIS ArcFlax 9” gives a closer view of the Trust’s work before the Whanganui DVD. The 43-slide deck credits Duane Wilkins at CFRT, describes ArcFlax 9 as participatory GIS for presenting evidence in a judicial inquiry, and identifies ArcReader 9.1. A later presentation by Wilkins describes a 2004–2007 DVD series for Waitangi Tribunal inquiry districts and a then-current all-Aotearoa ArcFlax 2.0 resource kete stored in Google Drive. These records document a wider programme and a named practitioner, but they do not establish the exact coverage or layers on the Whanganui disc.

blocks.text: One route to wider GIS use still depended on a disc rather than a website. The Crown Forestry Rental Trust published ArcFlax Edition 2.0 Whanganui in 2006 as an interactive GIS DVD. The National Library's catalogue credits Duane Wilkins and specifies ArcReader 9.1, a free Esri viewer, as a system requirement. It is a documented example of packaging prepared geographic information for Treaty research without requiring the recipient to own a full desktop GIS authoring package. The catalogue identifies this edition and its format but does not describe every dataset on the disc or establish when an earlier edition first appeared.

blocks.text: A January 2007 quick-start guide supplies implementation details for Northland Edition 1.0. It says ArcFlax was the map data; users installed ArcReader 9.1 separately, copied the DVD folder to the root of C:\\, and opened the 2D or 3D projects there. The stated minimum was Windows XP or similar, a DVD drive, 5 GB free space and 256 MB RAM. The guide limits use to contracted CFRT clients for Treaty-settlement purposes, says the DVD was intended to support Northland claimant mapping planned for 2007–08, and lists seven project variants using the same source data, with all layers available only in the Deluxe editions. The guide includes a QuickStart tutorial and says CFRT could not provide ongoing installation or use support.

blocks.text: The guide names 75 cm aerial photography for Whangārei District; Natural Geographx textures for Northland; archaeological data maintained by DOC; Landcare Research’s LENZ-based predicted potential vegetation; land-use capability; LINZ Crown Licensed Forests, Core Record Set and Topo50k; Native Land Court parent-block boundaries drawn from original survey plans; Crown Purchase and Old Land Claim blocks captured for the Northland Technical Research Programme; 2001 deprivation and population data at meshblock scale; and Landsat imagery. It says 2006 Census data were expected in ArcFlax 2.0, but that forward-looking note does not prove their inclusion in the 2006 Whanganui Edition 2.0. These layer details belong to Northland 1.0 unless the Whanganui disc itself is examined.

blocks.text: A separate Tribunal archival record gives a clearer view of another ArcFlax package. The Te Paparahi o Te Raki inquiry register lists an ArcFlax 1.0 Northland two-dimensional and three-dimensional GIS viewer, dated January 2007 and held as five discs under entry A045. Its documented material includes Crown purchase maps, Old Land Claims, Native Land Court blocks and other historical map images. The register records the package as supplied by the Crown Forestry Rental Trust in December 2013. This Northland edition follows the catalogued 2006 Whanganui 'Edition 2.0' in calendar time, which shows why edition numbers cannot be treated as a single national release sequence. The five-disc record is evidence of geographic coverage and map categories, but its internal project files have not been inspected.

blocks.text: A related task-focused effort joined AgResearch and Landcare Research with Māori land organisations. From the Iwi Futures programme begun in late 2007, Garth Harmsworth and Alec Mackay developed a Land and Resource Evaluation module through case studies with Ngāti Hine Health Trust, Paehinahina-Mourea Trust, Waimarama Incorporation and Aohanga Incorporation. The work assembled land-block information, soil and other national datasets, field observations and owner questions into GIS knowledge repositories, thematic maps and reusable data layers. The 2010 paper describes a draft, step-by-step module for identifying resources and assessing development options; it does not prove that a public web service was launched. It also notes that cultural layers in the case-study repositories were confidential and access restricted.

blocks.text: A task-specific application reverses that emphasis. It begins with a defined task such as reviewing crime reported in an area, finding land-resource information for a place, recording completion of a safety check or documenting a support need at a location. The interface can then hide functions that do not contribute to that task. A user may never need to know which feature service supplies the map, which fields are stored in the database or which spatial operation is being performed. The application narrows the experience deliberately.

blocks.text: That narrowing can widen the audience. A general GIS is powerful because it can do many things, but that also makes it demanding. A person using it has to understand enough about both the software and the data to choose sensible operations. A purpose-built application can remove choices that are irrelevant to a particular user. The result may be less flexible, but it can also be faster to learn and much harder to misuse accidentally.

blocks.text: This changed the work of GIS practitioners. Requirements had to be understood before the interface was built. Designers had to establish what the user actually needed to decide, which terms belonged to the user’s ordinary work, which locations or categories were visible and which edits were allowed. A GIS analyst could no longer assume that exposing more layers or tools was automatically helpful. Application design required choosing what not to show.
